item.title: The Best Fly Patterns to Catch a Grand Slam
item.description: Catching a true grand slam—a permit, bonefish, and tarpon in a single day—is the epitome of saltwater fly fishing. Many anglers go their whole saltwater careers chasing a slam, traveling to far-off destinations in search of pristine habitat and abundant opportunities. One common destination to check off a grand slam is Belize.

item.title: Belize’s Most Overlooked Fish
item.description: Most fly anglers head to Belize in search of the big three: bonefish, permit, and tarpon. In terms of saltwater fly fishing, it’s one of the best locations to consistently have opportunities at a grand slam.

item.title: Meet the Crew: Alexandra Nicole
item.description: Anglers Alexandra Nicole and Alec Lucas head to Belize for season 2 of Coast 2 Coast. Their goal is to explore the different parts of the country, from shallow water flats to backwater lagoons, in search of the hardest thing to do in saltwater fly fishing: catch a grand slam (permit, bonefish, and tarpon).

item.title: The Double Figure 8 Loop knot
item.description: Loop knots give your fly superior action in the water. In the first of three videos on better salt water knots, Capt. Joel Dickey shows us how to tie the Double Figure 8 Loop Knot.

item.title: 3rd Time’s a Charm

item.title: Lionfish – Tasty on Pizza, Hell on the Ecosystem
item.description: Lionfish may be the mother of all invasive species. Take a moment to think about this: a lionfish (native to the Indo-Pacific) has no natural predators in the Atlantic ocean. It can live up to fifteen years, reaching sexual maturity in less than a year. Once mature, a pair can spawn as often as every four days.

item.title: Yamame
item.description: “Yamame” is a dwarf riverine form of cherry salmon/masu salmon (Oncorhynchus masou). Almost all Yamame are males, and they participate in spawning with sea-run females.On Sakhalin, we call them “podkamenka” (literally “under the rocks”). They inhabit mountain rivers in large numbers and bite well on all types of lures.

item.title: From Lakes to Lagoons: Your Saltwater Survival Guide
item.description:
Transitioning from freshwater to saltwater fishing might feel like learning to ride a bike again—except this time, you’ve got waves, salt, and maybe a shark or two. The insight from fellow anglers shows that while the fundamentals of casting and retrieving remain, the nuances of saltwater fishing require some tweaking. Whether you’re fishing the beaches of La Paz or the jungles of Costa Rica, adapting your skills is crucial.

Take, for example, the Reddit threads where anglers share their saltwater debut experiences. One newbie was thrown right into the chaos of feeding fish, learning that a fast retrieve and the right bait can make all the difference. Or consider the podcast with Kevin Jackson, packing in the reality that not only can you target tarpon and trout on the same trip, but you’ll also need to adjust your approach depending on the conditions. So, if you’ve been slinging flies for trout in your local river and think you’re ready for some salt, pay attention. There’s more to it than just casting into the waves and hoping for the best.
